content.title: Iowa States TJ Otzelberger declares commitment to Iowa State Im the coach of the Cyclones
content.text: Iowa State basketball coach T.J. Otzelberger declared his commitment to the Cyclones and Iowa State amid speculation about his name being linked to the head coaching opportunity at North Carolina CHICAGO – Amid his name being connected to the vacant head coaching job at North Carolina, fifth-year Iowa State head coach T.J. Otzelberger declared his commitment to Iowa State on Wednesday in the Cyclones' hotel prior to Friday's Sweet 16 game vs. No. 6 seed Tennessee."I'd just like to start by saying, any speculation with me and any other jobs or opportunities is not true," Otzelberger opened his presser with. "I'm the coach of the Cyclones. Thrilled to be the coach of the Cyclones."North Carolina fired Hubert Davis after five seasons leading the Tar Heels on Tuesday night. Davis was dismissed after the Tar Heels lost in the Round of 64 to No. 6 seed VCU. The Tar Heels blew a 19-point lead in the loss, contributing to Davis' firing after four NCAA Tournament appearances in five seasons. The Tar Heels lost the national championship game in Davis' first season to Kansas after earning a No. 8 seed in March Madness. Davis' team was the ACC champion in 2023-24, and they earned a No. 1 seed. But much of his tenure was viewed as falling short of UNC's lofty standards.Otzelberger, meanwhile, has become, arguably, the best coach in Iowa State history in a short amount of time. He is the only coach to lead Iowa State to five consecutive NCAA Tournament appearances, and this season's Sweet 16 appearance is the third under Otzelberger's direction. Iowa State has been ranked in the AP Top 25 since the mid-point of the 2023-24 season.With new Iowa State University president Dr. David Cook in place, Otzelberger feels supported at the highest levels of Iowa State's administration. He said he feels supported by long-time Iowa State athletic director Jamie Pollard."As we move forward together, the alignment on our campus with Dr. Cook, Jamie Pollard is amazing," Otzelberger said. "And we're thrilled about our future together. So, really appreciative and grateful to Jamie Pollard and David Cook and conversations we've had."Prior to the 2024-25 season, Otzelberger agreed to a fully guaranteed contract to coach at Iowa State through the 2032 season. If he were to accept a head coaching position at another school, the program would owe Iowa State $4 million for his hiring.Otzelberger's .7-5 winning percentage and .587 conference winning percentage are both the best in school history. Otzelberger has 30 wins over AP Top 25 ranked competition, which is the most of any coach in school history.Iowa State plays vs. Tennessee in the United Center on Friday at 9:10 p.m. CT on TBS.Coach Quotes: Tyler Roehl explains practice dynamics, standout players in early spring football practicesA full transcript of what Iowa State OC Tyler Roehl said in his Wednesday press conference AMES – Iowa State football is in the early stages of spring practices under first-year coach Jimmy Rogers. He is supported by offensive coordinator Tyler Roehl.On Wednesday, Roehl spoke with local reporters about his offense after three spring practices.On how early practices are going You know, yeah, I'm happy with where we're at in practice. I'm not satisfied for one second. There's a lot of good, but then it's just how consistent can you be? How are you able to practice with the championship habits, the finish, the effort, the physicality, every single rep? That's what's demanded.And no, there's glimpses of really good, but then there's glimpses of we have a long ways to go. So I'm happy. I'm just not satisfied.On getting the offense to mesh amid so many new players Change can be hard, but change can have unbelievable growth. And with this group, I mean, you're just teaching from ground level, just the base fundamentals of football. And for all of us to be in alignment and on the same page of what's desired, what's wanted, what's necessary for us to have success on scheme A, scheme B, scheme C. I mean, there's just a lot of teaching that goes into it.And you just go down to the level of trust and connection that's needed within the roster to execute a play, to have all 11 on the same page with each and every scheme. And there's a lot that's put on the quarterback's plate. Like you can check plays and schemes based off the front, based off numbers, based off safety structure, based off rotation, based off a lot of things. So just for them to handle everything at the line of scrimmage can be a lot. And then to communicate that to the other 10 on the field. But again, we're grasping it well. We need to have urgency.On the energy of players and coaches chasing the ball in practice Oh, that's the standard. And that's the expectation. You know, from a player standpoint, you're going to feed off of the energy of the coach. And if we're just standing there with our hands in our pockets, well, how is the player going to be energized and ready to play?I think we as coaches set the tone with how we approach, shoot, the time they walk into the building, in the meetings. Do we have positive contagious energy for them to learn from? Because coaching is teaching. Teaching is to inspire learning. How can we inspire them to grow, to learn?And then, no, I appreciate the heck out of the offensive staff. Right? I'm trying to get the organization, the structure, the next personnel grouping in so we can get as many repetitions as we want within the practice. Now you see Coach (Derrick) Sherman flying down the field, Coach (Jake) Thornton.I mean, the players feed off of that. It doesn't need to be like fake juice, fake energy. It needs to be real and authentic. If that play is a good play, go run after them. If it's not, well, let's go and coach as they're coming back to the huddle and hold them accountable for whether it be a wrong first step or pad level or what have you, a route. No, I just think if there's a good play, let's bring good juice. If it's not a good play, well, let's just coach them as they're on the way back to the huddle.On handling reps between players at practice You can't get enough reps, as many as possible. That's why we've gone to the mode of double repping. At practice, you're going to see really two practices going on. One group's on one end running plays, one group's on the other end running plays.And, you know, my philosophy has always been, our philosophy is, that you can't learn by just standing there. I can't tell a kid, make sure you're learning that, and he just standing there watching, but never actually in there doing it. And so, if they're actually physically in there taking the repetition, okay, they're going to learn from it. They're going to learn from doing the rep, getting coached on the way back to the huddle, in the meeting room, okay, watching themselves do it. And by the time you're done with a spring ball and a fall camp with this model of double repping, you should have run every single scheme versus about any look that you could see out of this defense and feel really prepared, become, you know, the end of August to be ready to go.So, the way in which we're practicing, the way in which Coach Rogers has scheduled out how we're doing spring ball and then into fall camp, this is unbelievable for us to grow, to learn, and to get as many repetitions as possible as we, you know, go through spring ball because it's needed.On how many reps a player could get in a spring practice Oh man, within a practice, you could probably get anywhere from 40 to 50 reps. That's in a team setting. So, then you take that times 15 and I am not smart enough right now to do that math, but that's a lot, you know, that's a lot.And that's why you're seeing growth. And the hard thing in spring ball, right, is from an offensive standpoint, you have this schedule of how you're going to install the schemes.Day one is this run scheme and pass schemes. So, okay, but also we know what the defense is doing on day one and vice versa. So, everyone knows what's going in on that day. So, it's probably the hardest to execute that scheme because they know exactly what's coming. And then you get to get day two and they know what's going in and we know what's going in. Day three, everybody knows what's going in. So, it's challenging. So, if you can execute it on those days, you feel pretty good about those schemes.Once you get to about day seven, eight of spring ball, where everything's in, that's where you, okay, we can really hang our hat on that. You know, practice seven, eight, nine, ten, you're executing that at a high level. You can hang your hat on those schemes that you're executing because really they don't know. I mean, everything's in. They got to defend it, but we also have to be ready for what they have defensively as well.On players who have impressed him at practice Okay, I'm going to start at quarterback and there's three that are doing really well, really well. You know, Jaylen (Raynor), Connor (Moberly), and Zane (Flores) are all playing at a high level. And I didn't say it in that order for any reason, but they're all playing at a high level and grasping everything. Their athletic ability, they're doing a good job.Running back wise, you know, two guys that I had here in 2024, you got Easton Miller and Aiden Flora. You know, Easton could do a number of things if he can handle it mentally, you know, from playing out on the perimeter to playing in the core and then playing true tailback. Same thing with Aiden Flora. I mean, you're going to split Aiden Flora. I know, shoot, when I was here, we used him at wildcat quarterback. And then Salahadin (Allah) is doing a good job and so is Cameron Pettaway. Cam's playing at a high level and Cam can be very multiple for us.Going to tight end, Vince Benetti, Keaton Roskop, Christian Greenlaw, Cash Hayden's doing some good things, just the consistency needs to be there. A.J. Petersen, I mean, could have a role as a fullback and block. You know, I think he's doing a good job. Tyler Fortenberry, then you got some young guys in there that are just trying to figure it out, but their urgency to learn is noticeable.Receiver, Dom Overby, Evan Boyd, Jordan Bailey, Cody Jackson, Omari Hayes, Carter Pabst, I'm drawing a blank. That group, I think the receiver group is really talented right now and they're working their tails off.Line-wise, it's going to be deep as well, but I'm going to go Gibby, Gabe Greenlee, DeAndre Carter, Colin Amick, Braden Smith, Jake Taylor, Garret Rutledge, (Austin) Barrett, I should have said that one right away.And I know I'm going to miss three guys there, so I apologize, guys, but you know, I just, we've, we've got good depth, we do, but who's going to separate themselves as we go through these 15 practices going into the fall? And that's what's exciting, because right now to be able to put together a complete depth chart, good luck. I mean, we've only had one practice, a full pad, that rest is you've got helmets on and spiders, and it's not real football at the end of the day. And when you got full pads on, that's real football, and it's when you can figure out who's about it and who's not. And we got guys that are about it.I don't know if we're going to win a game, two games, but you have a group in a locker room that is willing to play with physicality, high effort, encourage their teammates, like that's what's exciting for me. We got the right guys. Now it's just the football side of things to get everyone going in the right direction.On what he has seen from PettawayYeah, I hope you get a lot of words out of him because he's pretty quiet. He's pretty quiet, but I appreciate him. He's high IQ, works his tail off, highly competitive. He's starting to just, you know, even, you know, break the cusp of adding more on his plate. You know, he's, I mean, it's not like he doesn't belong. He belongs. He's playing at a high level. I think you do a lot of stuff out in the backfield. Where can we add more to his plate in terms of things outside of the court and on the perimeter?On the challenge of getting players aligned Yeah, get all those tools in alignment and demand one thing, and that's to play with physicality. And like I said, we got guys that are about it and that want to play with it.And honestly, right now, if you're not playing with that mentality, that mindset, you kind of don't belong right now on the field because 98% of the guys are playing with that. And it's pretty glaring if you don't. And that's the standard. That's the expectation. Even if we have a really good run in the middle of practice, I don't need every single player running down to the end zone. I don't. Because for me and what I've been a part of, that's the expectation. Let's get back in the huddle. Let's call another play. Let's go. And so I appreciate the enjoyment and the joy that we have within a good play. But it's not like on first and 10 and we break one for 30, we can all just go run and celebrate. I mean, it's got to be a touchdown. So we need to get ready to play the next play as well. But know that to be able to dictate the terms of engagement in the game, you must control the ground to control the air.And them embodying that, embracing that mentality of a sprint to hit mindset, that's the standard.On the three QBs individually Yeah. Okay. Let's start with Zane. Okay. Zane is high football IQ. He's one that plays in rhythm, in time with his sets, with his communication at the line of scrimmage, the command and poise in the huddle, truly being the quarterback and distributing the ball where it needs to be on time with accuracy. Has good athletic ability, ability to run the ball, create maybe an off-schedule play with the ball in his hands and scramble.Moberly is uber athletic. Was a running back, you know, a lot in youth football. I think he told me that was a year and a half ago, but very capable thrower of the football. I think his processing is on par with where he should be. I just want more urgency with it, but very capable. He's done a really good job.And then Jaylen, good athlete, plays in time and rhythm. He has unbelievable leadership, like him in the locker room, in the hallways, anywhere, like you will rarely, if ever, see him without a smile on his face. Like that's infectious. Like I appreciate that about him. I'm excited to see as we go through, you know, our installation of spring ball to see like what throws he can play and play in time and precision and what throws are hard for him.But I'm excited where they're all at. I really am.On how much Raynor is a QB and doesn't just act like a QB Yeah, like it's everything in terms of going to class, showing up, up in the lunchroom, in a meeting.Like I was around one of the best last year in (Jared) Goff, like how truly professional he was. And I'm even talking about just in a walkthrough and the standards that he had at the walkthrough. Like if we were going to the line of scrimmage and something was off, 'Hey, re-huddle. Wasn't good enough.'And okay, even a pass route, just how he's working through his drop and precision and time. And it's all that. It's truly being obsessed with the details of what it means to be a quarterback, to be the CEO of the offense, to be the face of the program.It's not just showing up and I'm just going to go and throw the ball around. And also, there's so much that goes into it. And that's what I've appreciated. These are high level, mature individuals that we have. And it's just continuing to hold that standard of, to play quarterback in this system, there's a lot on your plate. You need to be curious to learn. Curious to learn, okay, maybe where to set the protection, how to set the protection. Why are we setting the protection that way? Understanding the front, understanding backers and tandems and what that may present. Tips on safety rotation. I mean, there's so much that goes into it and you need to be curious and obsessed with learning, but urgent to learn. So that's what's fun in teaching. I think this level is there, you can teach them so much. And then how fast can they grasp it? And there's a lot of time starting from scratch. Good things though, these guys are from really good high school programs. So they have a really good foundation to build upon.Coach Quotes: Jesse Bobbit shares how players are adapting to a new defense at Iowa StateA full transcript of everything Iowa State defensive coordinator Jessee Bobbit said about this defense in his press conference on Wednesday afternoon AMES – Iowa State football completed its third practice of spring football on Tuesday and its first practice in pads. This is the first year under head coach Jimmy Rogers, who is supported by defensive coordinator Jesse Bobbit and offensive coordinator Tyler Roehl.Bobbit met with local media on Wednesday to discuss his defensive unit. Below is a full transcript of the press conference. On how things are going in the program, on his defense Yeah, things are definitely starting to feel normal. I think the camaraderie within the staff has been great. Obviously, on the defensive side of the ball, we've been together for a while. Obviously, you've had a couple new pieces with Coach (Ross) Watson and some of the assistant coaches by position, but things are coming together really well on our side of the ball, for sure.In terms of how we're getting along with the offense, it's not good, I'm just kidding. No, things are good. Getting along well. Love the culture that they're instilling on that side of the ball, and the effort and the mentality they have.It's been a fun few practices so far. I was going to put the pads on yesterday, but things are definitely feeling normal. I think everyone's feeling pretty settled, and it's been fun so far.On practicing with the offense Yeah, we've been doing a lot of team. I feel like we've been doing team. It feels like the last two months in some of these walkthroughs and stuff, but it's been really competitive, both sides of the ball. There's not just 11 guys on each side running the ball. There's like four or five coaches also running to the ball on each side, and so that's been fun. Love to see the spirit and energy that both sides have from a coaching standpoint, and really pushing the guys to be at their best and have great effort.Coaching the details. Coach (Jimmy) Rogers is big into coaching between plays, and get your butt off the field so you can give him the space. So we're running on and off, trying to coach as much as possible.On the dynamic of coaching the defense with transfers who understand it and players who are learning the scheme for the first time Yeah, no, it's been really good. I think guys have been really open, the guys that were able to come with us and understand how we operate and what we do. Not only us as coaches bringing guys in and showing them, it's huge that there's players that are able to do that. I think the biggest thing from a team perspective, but also on the defensive side of the ball, giving the guys opportunities to talk to each other and lead. We're unit meeting as a defense a few times a week, and in those unit meetings, it's not just X's and O's. It is a lot of the culture building and camaraderie piece and guys getting to know one another each day.We have guys come up and talk in front of the group, and usually I'm each day strategically picking someone that was already here, someone that came with us from Wazu, and then someone who is from somewhere else. Just having guys continue to get to know each other and that allows the bond to come together.We've done a lot of things the last couple months from a culture building, from a whole team perspective, with Kris Kracht and Coach Rogers. It's made it seem like if you're at practice or you're anywhere around the building that these guys have been with each other for a year or two and that you wouldn't notice that it's been only a couple months, which has been fun.On the fun of spring practices No, it's been awesome. It's definitely fun, and it's been a great challenge, I think, as a coach. When you look at it, having a new roster, reinstalling everything like everyone's a freshman, getting coaches on the same page, that is the fun because of the challenge of trying to get everyone to the level of which we want to be and coaching at that standard and playing at that standard.So it's been a ton of fun, and as you can tell by my voice, it's a little hoarse just in terms of screaming and yelling and trying to be loud and getting in on the action to coach the guys up and get back out. So my voice is struggling a little bit, but it's been fun.On using Washington State transfers to teach the defense Yeah, I talked a little bit about the culture piece, but from a schematic standpoint, they're usually the ones getting some of the first reps, and so the guys can watch that. Some of the teach tape that we're using actually is from Washington State, and so they're watching those guys do it where there's something to that, right? And then you watch the guy who's sitting next to you do it on a day from a different school. You feel more comfortable asking him the questions. 'Hey, why did you do that?' Or 'What was the mistake there? I don't get it.' Whatever it is, right?So, it's a huge advantage having guys that have already done it. Those guys can lean on them and watch those reps be done, whether that's indie or team or in a meeting. Whatever it is, whatever a coach expects, those guys can lead the way and catch guys up, and we're all working on patching.On how returning players help build the culture Yeah, I think it's awesome. I think specifically just talking about the defense and us as coaches, we have zero ego. So we talk about doing this together, and so we have what we do, what we've done. But I always ask the guys that have been here in a different scheme, wherever they came from, 'Hey, what have you guys done?' Or 'How are you taught this so I know how you were taught?' 'That makes sense why you're doing that because you've been taught that for three years.' All right, 'Well, here's how we can adjust, and here's how I can make it same as for you in teaching.' And so I think there's that aspect of it.But I think what's been really cool, at least in the linebacker room for sure, we've got some guys that were here like Carson Willich. He's asking a ton of questions and really good intellectual curiosity, I would call it, where he's always taking one step farther, and that makes the group better. That makes me better as a coach. And sometimes they'll catch you off guard with some of the things they ask, like 'Where did that come from?' But it's good. They're thinking, which is fun.On balancing competition and learning the defense Yeah, there's no doubt. And so it's been an evaluation since they got here. So is there like a set depth chart? No, but when you talk about who's going out there with the first group, there is a little bit of a depth chart, and the guys see that, and that's based off the evaluation since we got here and they got back from winter break or whoever, when they came in as a transfer, of how they're doing in walkthroughs, how they've been in meetings, what they're showing up, if they're doing things right, and being on time with the things.If they're one of the guys that's on the list, they're probably not going out there first, even if they are the most talented, because right now we gotta learn and everything's an evaluation. Are you accountable? And so you're trying to balance it all, but we're definitely evaluating everything, and that's a play into who's going out there first and who's getting the most reps, and that's day-to-day.I think right now from all positions defensively, I know we're intermixing guys and having him get reps with him. It's not like you two are the ones until you're not. I'm continuing to mix guys up and working with each other, because you never know. You want them all to be able to communicate together, who works well together, make it a fair competition and fair evaluation in terms of maybe someone ends up taking reps finally with someone who's a great communicator and can help him get aligned and that person starts playing better, and they get more reps and actually learn better.So it's good to mix it up for now, and then as things go, I think I would see it being that way through spring ball for the most part.Maybe on a scrimmage day, it would set up a little bit more depth chart-wise, but by the time you get to fall, that's when I would say evaluations aren't done, but you have a pretty good idea of what your depth chart would be.On who some of the standouts players have been Yeah, I would say starting up front, Bryson Lamb and Isaac Terrell. Bobby, they call him. Bobby Boucher. But those two stand out up front, and a little bit of that comes from some of the questions that we've had of the carryover. Naturally, you would think those guys, with the talented players that they are, but also the mental carryover of running this defense, they've been standing out in a big positive way.I would say Caden Crawford up front as well. From USD has been what we would hope for, and he needs to just keep doing what he's doing and keep taking it day by day and being at his best.Going down the list at linebacker, I've been really happy with Malcolm Jones and Willie Breland, they're at SAM/nickel, and they've been taking a lot of reps just based off of the amount of bodies we have at that position, and they're working their tails off, and they're trying to have 100% pursuit every down to the ball, but they're running a lot. But I've been proud with those guys at linebacker.Tristan Exline, who we brought in from UTPB, is doing a lot these last couple days as the mental side of the game is really starting to click for him. You can see some of the things he saw on film, which we were really excited about him triggering, playing faster. The physicality piece yesterday was awesome to see out of him.And then at linebacker, I would say maybe the most consistent one right now is Carson Willich. He's been eager since day one when we got here asking questions, being in the building, watching film, all the things, and he's executing at a really high level. So that's been awesome to see out of him because usually when you put in the work and the time and all the things, it's cool to see it actually happen out there.You're excited for that. And then at the back end, Braden Awls is doing some really good things. His athleticism and natural. He's played a lot of football, and so you can see that out there. It's fun to now see it in spring ball, just his instincts and being in the right place. And yesterday, seeing his physicality, that was really cool to see, along with the whole safety group had a really good day yesterday, but Xavier Martinez, guys coming in, and Duhron (Goodman) and (Micah) Harper. So that group.And then at corner, got some length. I feel really good about that position and the depth that we've had. It's more depth than we've ever had, wherever I've been, at the corner position. And so David Coffey got some really good coverage ability in that whole group. And then the next aspect of what we're going to ask our corners to do is fit and run. So you also need to be physical, and I would say the natural question at times is people ask, 'Well, is the corner physical or not?' He's been showing up with some great physicality, along with some other guys.So those are some guys that just come to mind, as I'd say it, but there's a lot of pieces in here that I could go through in detail and say why they're progressing or having a really good winter and spring so far.On Willich Yeah, in my opinion, it does. I think this scheme does fit him a little bit more in allowing him to play with a little bit more freedom. Since I've been coaching, our WILL linebacker position that he's playing in this defense is set up to have a lot of success and be able to make a lot of plays or be in positions to make those plays.You also have to be very physical. So when you look at what traits and ability does he have to bring to the table, one is his physicality in setting edges or attacking the ball and spilling or bouncing a puller. He does that with some intent and some violence, which is awesome.He's been a great communicator since we've been here. So he's helping guys get aligned. He hasn't had too many mental errors at all or missed assignments because he's studying and he's communicating and getting guys on the right page.But then also with how we play our defense, our linebackers, in comparison to what he's been playing in previously, are allowed to scrape more and play at depth more and trigger on things and maybe, not as much hole-pluggers as they maybe were last year or previously within that scheme. I think he's going to have a lot of opportunities to make plays and it definitely fits him. He's very well-rounded within his ability and it's been fun.His issue is he's been injured a lot of his career at different times, and so he's healthy right now and we'll try to keep him that way.On a sense of urgency for players Yeah, no doubt. And we experienced that a little bit last year for sure, but just talking about here now, there's definitely some urgency out there. There's no one that is a, 'Hey, you're the starter.' That's at any position, offense or defense. It is known that everyone's competing and we're going to be competing until week one to be the guy, and that's ever-changing.And so it is fun to see that competition, but there's also that chip on the shoulder from a six-year senior that transferred in, I think Max (Baloun) was a seventh-year senior, or the true freshman that enrolled early. No one has like, 'Well, this is my spot.' No one has that ego or mentality. It's like everyone's fighting for it with joy and no sinking their heads or holding their heads down because they didn't get a rep right now.Earn your reps. And so guys are learning that they need to earn their reps and execute. Whether you get 10 reps or 20 reps, make the most of your reps and you'll earn more.On how big of a scheme change Iowa State is making Yeah, definitely a big change. Big change.It's a big change to go from a three-down to a four-down in general. When you talk about the box structure and how you fit runs and, you know, coverages are the same in a lot of ways. It just makes it look different no matter what scheme you're in.But from a front standpoint and how we play our front at times, which is different than other four-down teams, mixing it up, it changes it up quite a bit. And so, you know, again, I really believe in our scheme and what it allows that position to do and have a lot of success. And, you know, Carson's a great example of, he's like, 'Man, I really love this defense.'He loves the freedom that he has and he likes the responsibility that he has in being out of the box, in the box, different paths, blitzing, all the things. So, it's definitely different and excited for those guys to be able to showcase and keep learning and hopefully be a big part of our success on defense.On the challenge of learning a new system as a defensive lineman, like Zaimir Hawk is being asked to do Yeah, it's definitely a challenge. Yeah, no matter how smart you are with this or you can learn the playbook like that, just doing the reps, it's way different. You know, he was zero nose. And then a lot of times you're just getting vertical off the rock. Now he's got to read things. We're popping with pullers.He can be stuck, like he could be a shade. He could be a 2i. He could be a three. Like they're going to do it all. Like our d-linemen really across the board, depending on what we do and what we eventually get to, are asked to really be able to play any defensive position across the board, all four. They're not playing safety, sorry. I wouldn't ask that out of him.So yes, it is a learning curve for sure. And so, I mean, from where he was at a couple weeks ago or a month ago in walkthroughs to where he was at yesterday, huge difference. And it just takes reps. It just takes reps.And I'd love to shout out him, as you asked about him too. It's just his leadership and him speaking and opening up in those unit meetings and being someone that's trying to be a leader on this defense. It's been cool to see.
